common_mistakes: Adding soy sauce and miso at the very start of a long simmer, so their fragrance cooks away before serving.
Putting ginger in at the beginning of a simmered dish when its aroma is meant to arrive fresh at the end.
Seasoning everything in one go without a final adjustment after the dish has rested and cooled.
Using a single miso for everything and missing the depth that a blend provides.
Adding the teriyaki sauce early and simmering the chicken in it, which burns the sugars, softens the crisp skin and flattens the glaze.
Salting fish from directly above the surface, so the salt lands in uneven patches and the seasoning comes out spotty.
core_principles: The mnemonic Sa-Shi-Su-Se-So orders seasonings by how they behave: sugar (sa) first because it penetrates ingredients slowly and needs the head start.
Salt (shi) comes after sugar, since salt pulls moisture out of ingredients and would block the sugar if it went first.
Vinegar (su) goes in later because its sharp edge softens with heat, so it is kept away from long cooking.
Soy sauce (se) follows because its fragrance fades with prolonged heating.
Miso (so) comes last because its aroma is the most delicate of all and dies first in the heat.
Temperature difference is a seasoning tool: hot food plunged into cooled sauce absorbs flavor faster, because the sauce is pulled in as the food cools.
Vinegar has two opposite jobs: early in a long simmer it is a worker that tenderizes bones and strips odor, while late in cooking it is a perfume that must be protected from heat.

key_facts: Sa-Shi-Su-Se-So stands for sugar (satou), salt (shio), vinegar (su), soy sauce (shouyu, from the old 'se' reading) and miso (miso, from 'so').
In simmered mackerel with miso, the grated ginger is deliberately not added at the start; it goes in near the end so its aroma stays alive.
Simmered dishes take up most of their flavor while cooling, through osmotic pressure, which is why final seasoning is judged after the dish rests rather than at a rolling boil.
Sukiyaki's sauce, warishita, is pre-mixed from kombu dashi, soy sauce, sake, sugar and mirin so the balance is fixed before it ever meets the pan.
Blending two misos, a regular miso with a portion of red miso, gives a mellow depth that is rich without becoming heavy.
For pickled cucumbers, the vinegar dressing is applied twice: the first round draws out the remaining moisture and the second round sets the pure flavor, so the taste stays clear over time.
Fresh aromatics are treated like late seasonings throughout the sources: ginger goes into simmered fish at the finish, never at the start.
A little Worcestershire sauce whisked into teriyaki tare is a classic secret ingredient: a teaspoon or two adds spice complexity and depth that soy sauce and mirin alone do not have.
A Western-style sauce for chicken katsu is built exactly like a tare: red wine, mirin, soy sauce and ketchup in equal parts, simmered down until it thickens and turns glossy.
For beef tataki, vinegar is splashed over the meat while it is still hot from searing and patted in with the fingertips, cutting the fat and clearing away any gaminess before the ponzu goes on.
Salt for grilled fish is sprinkled from about 20 centimeters above the surface, so it falls in an even rain instead of landing in salty patches.

Chicken and burdock for tatsuta-age are marinated together in the same ginger, soy and mirin mixture, so the burdock's earthy aroma moves into the chicken and the two fry up tasting like one ingredient.
Sukiyaki does not start with its sauce: the green onions are seared first to draw out their sweetness and the beef is briefly grilled, and only then does the warishita meet the pan.
A spoonful of mirin stirred in at the very end of a miso soup leaves a soft, lingering sweetness and rounds out the miso, without the soup ever tasting sugary.
Sugar itself can be the first thing cooked: heated in the pan until it caramelizes, it rounds out a tomato's acidity and gives a simple stir-fry a deep, complex base note.
Sardines for shigureni simmer for a full hour in vinegar water before any soy sauce or sugar is added, because the acid needs that time alone to soften the bones and carry away the fishiness.

practical_steps: In a simmered dish, add the sugar first and give it a few minutes before the salt follows.
Hold vinegar, soy sauce and miso back toward the end of cooking to protect their aroma.
Add fresh ginger in the final minutes of simmering fish instead of at the beginning.
Let a simmered dish cool once and taste again before deciding it needs more seasoning.
Try blending a spoonful of red miso into your usual miso for extra depth without extra saltiness.
Treat teriyaki sauce as a glaze, not a bath: add it only after the chicken skin is crisp, toss until glossy, and take the pan off the heat.
Use ginger twice in simmered fish: slices in the pot for the cooking, and a tuft of fine raw shreds on top at serving for the fresh aroma.
When a fried dish will be soaked in sauce, cool the sauce first and add the food while it is still hot from the oil.
Sprinkle salt on fish from a height of about 20 centimeters for an even coating.
scene: A grandmother's simmer pot on the stove, seasonings lined up beside it in a row, each one waiting for its turn to go in.
theme: Sa-Shi-Su-Se-So is the traditional order of seasoning in Japanese cooking, sugar, salt, vinegar, soy sauce, miso, arranged so each one can do its job and the delicate aromas survive to the table.
viewer_takeaways: Seasoning has an order for a reason: what penetrates slowly goes first, and what smells delicate goes last.
Aromatics like ginger and miso belong at the end of cooking, not the beginning.
Let simmered food rest and cool once before judging whether it needs more salt.
When a seasoning goes in matters as much as which one: the same ingredient can tenderize, glaze or perfume depending on its moment.
